courses.title: Python Fundamentals for Data Analysis
courses.summary: A practical first course in Python for officials who will work with statistical data files.
outcomes: Write short Python programs using variables, lists and dictionaries
Use loops, conditions and functions to process records
Read a CSV file and compute simple totals

lessons.title: Values, variables and types
body: Python stores every piece of data as a **value** with a type. The types you will use most for data work are `int` (whole numbers), `float` (decimals), `str` (text) and `bool` (True/False).
A **variable** is a name that points to a value. Assigning creates or rebinds the name:
Collections group values together:
- A **list** is an ordered sequence: `ages = [23, 41, 37]`. Index from 0, so `ages[0]` is 23.
- A **dictionary** maps keys to values: `hh = {"id": 17, "size": 5}`; read with `hh["size"]`.
Use `type(x)` whenever you are unsure what a value is. Many data bugs come from numbers stored as text ("42" is a `str`, not an `int`).

lessons.title: Control flow and functions
body: A `for` loop repeats a block for each item in a collection. An `if` statement runs a block only when a condition is true.
A **function** packages logic under a name so you can reuse and test it. `def` defines it and `return` sends a result back:
Keep functions small and give them names that describe the result. Indentation (four spaces) defines which lines belong inside a loop, condition or function.

lessons.title: Reading a data file
body: Survey extracts usually arrive as CSV files. The standard `csv` module reads them row by row as dictionaries:

code: total += int(row["members"])   # convert text to int

body: Note two habits: open files with `with` so they close automatically, and convert text fields to numbers explicitly.
In the next course you will switch to **pandas**, which reads a whole file into a table (a DataFrame) in one line - but the ideas here explain what it does for you.

questions.text: What is the type of the value produced by `1250 * 4.3`?
questions.explanation: Multiplying an int by a float gives a float (5375.0).

questions.text: Given `ages = [23, 41, 37]`, what does `ages[1]` return?
questions.explanation: Lists are indexed from 0, so index 1 is the second item, 41.

questions.text: What does `return` do inside a function?
options: Sends a result back to the caller
questions.explanation: `return` ends the function and hands its result to whoever called it.

questions.text: For `sizes = [3, 6, 2, 8, 4]`, how many items satisfy `s >= 6`?
questions.explanation: Only 6 and 8 are at least 6.

questions.text: Why is `int(row["members"])` needed when reading a CSV with csv.DictReader?
options: CSV values are read as text
questions.explanation: csv.DictReader returns every field as a string; convert explicitly before doing arithmetic.

courses.title: Statistics and Sampling Fundamentals
courses.summary: Core descriptive statistics and the sampling ideas behind every official survey estimate.
outcomes: Choose and compute appropriate measures of centre and spread
Explain why random samples allow inference about a population
Interpret a sampling weight and a standard error

lessons.title: Centre and spread
body: The **mean** is the arithmetic average; the **median** is the middle value once data are sorted. For skewed data such as household income, a few very large values pull the mean upward, so the median is usually the better summary of a 'typical' household.
Spread describes how far values sit from the centre:
- **Range** = maximum - minimum. Simple, but driven entirely by two extreme values.
- **Variance** is the average squared deviation from the mean; the **standard deviation (SD)** is its square root and is in the original units.
- The **interquartile range (IQR)** = Q3 - Q1 covers the middle 50% and is robust to outliers.
Example: for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5 and the population SD is 2.

lessons.title: Populations, samples and randomness
body: A **population** is every unit we want to describe (all households in a state). A **sample** is the subset we actually observe. A **statistic** computed from the sample estimates the population **parameter**.

Samples only support reliable inference if units are selected by a known random mechanism. In **simple random sampling (SRS)** every unit has the same chance of selection. In **stratified sampling** the population is divided into strata (e.g. rural/urban) and a random sample is drawn in each, which improves precision and guarantees coverage of every stratum.
When units have unequal selection probabilities, each sampled unit carries a **sampling weight** equal to 1 / (probability of selection) - the number of population units it represents.

lessons.title: How precise is an estimate?
body: Different random samples give slightly different estimates. The **standard error (SE)** measures that sample-to-sample variation. For a sample mean under SRS, SE = SD / sqrt(n).
Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error - precision grows with the square root of n, not with n.
A 95% **confidence interval** is approximately estimate +/- 1.96 x SE. It is a statement about the method: intervals built this way capture the true parameter in about 95% of repeated samples.

questions.text: Monthly household incomes are strongly right-skewed. Which summary best describes a typical household?
questions.explanation: The median is not pulled up by a few very large incomes.

questions.text: What is the mean of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9?
questions.explanation: The sum is 40 over 8 values, so the mean is 5.

questions.text: Which measure of spread is least affected by outliers?
questions.explanation: The IQR only uses the middle 50% of the data.

questions.text: A household selected with probability 1/250 has a sampling weight of:
options: It depends on the household size
questions.explanation: The weight is the inverse of the selection probability: it represents 250 households.

questions.text: What is the main advantage of stratifying by rural/urban before sampling?
options: It removes the need for weights
It guarantees coverage of both groups and usually improves precision
questions.explanation: Stratification ensures each stratum is represented and typically lowers the standard error.

questions.text: If the sample size is multiplied by 4 (SRS), the standard error of the mean:
questions.explanation: SE = SD / sqrt(n); sqrt(4) = 2, so the SE halves.

courses.title: SQL and Data Management
courses.summary: Query, join and aggregate administrative and survey tables with SQL.
outcomes: Filter and sort rows with SELECT ... WHERE ... ORDER BY
Aggregate with GROUP BY and filter groups with HAVING
Combine tables with INNER and LEFT JOINs

lessons.title: Selecting and filtering
body: A relational table stores one kind of record per row, with typed columns. `SELECT` chooses columns, `WHERE` filters rows and `ORDER BY` sorts:
`WHERE` is applied before any grouping, row by row. Text values go in single quotes. Use `IS NULL`, not `= NULL`, to find missing values.

lessons.title: Aggregation
body: Aggregate functions - `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` - collapse many rows into one. `GROUP BY` produces one output row per group:

code: SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS villages, SUM(households) AS hh

body: `HAVING` filters **groups** after aggregation, whereas `WHERE` filters **rows** before it. `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(column)` skips NULLs.

lessons.title: Joining tables
body: Data are normalised into several tables linked by keys. A **join** re-combines them:
- `INNER JOIN` keeps only rows with a match in both tables.
- `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row from the left table and fills unmatched right-hand columns with NULL - useful for finding records that are missing in another source.

code: LEFT JOIN survey_allocation s ON s.district_code = d.district_code;

body: Always check row counts before and after a join; an unexpected increase usually means the join key is not unique.

questions.text: Which clause filters individual rows before any grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.text: How do you find rows where `pincode` is missing?
questions.explanation: NULL is never equal to anything; use IS NULL.

questions.text: You need states whose total households exceed 100,000. Where does that condition go?
questions.explanation: The condition is on an aggregate, so it belongs in HAVING.

questions.text: Which join keeps every district even if it has no survey allocation?
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps all rows of the left table and fills gaps with NULL.

questions.text: After a join the row count unexpectedly doubles. The most likely cause is:
options: The join key is not unique in one table
questions.explanation: Duplicate keys multiply matching rows.

courses.title: Python for Statistical Computing
courses.summary: Use pandas and SciPy to clean survey data, compute weighted estimates and run basic tests.
outcomes: Load, clean and reshape survey tables with pandas
Compute grouped and weighted estimates
Run and interpret a two-sample t-test with SciPy

lessons.title: DataFrames and cleaning
body: A pandas **DataFrame** is a table with labelled columns. Most work follows load -> inspect -> clean:

code: df = df.dropna(subset=["age"])  # drop rows missing age

body: Select columns with `df[["a", "b"]]`, filter rows with a boolean mask such as `df[df["sector"] == "Rural"]`. `.loc[rows, cols]` selects by label.
Prefer explicit cleaning steps you can re-run over manual edits in a spreadsheet: the script becomes documentation of what was done.

lessons.title: Grouped and weighted estimates
body: `groupby` splits the table, applies a function to each group and combines the results:
Survey records carry weights, so an unweighted mean describes the **sample**, not the population. A weighted mean is sum(w * x) / sum(w):
Always state whether a published figure is weighted - the two can differ substantially when some strata were over-sampled.

lessons.title: Testing a difference
body: To ask whether two groups differ beyond sampling noise, use a two-sample t-test. **Welch's** version does not assume equal variances and is the safer default:

The **p-value** is the probability of a difference at least this large *if there were truly no difference*. A small p (e.g. < 0.05) is evidence against 'no difference'; it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about whether the difference is large enough to matter.

questions.text: Which pandas call shows column types and non-null counts?
questions.explanation: df.info() lists dtypes and non-null counts per column.

questions.text: How do you keep only rural rows?
questions.explanation: A boolean mask inside [] keeps the rows where the condition is True.

questions.text: Values 10 and 20 have weights 3 and 1. What is the weighted mean?
Why can an unweighted survey mean mislead?
options: It describes the sample, not the population, when selection probabilities differ
questions.explanation: Over-sampled groups get too much influence unless weights are applied.

questions.text: A t-test gives p = 0.01. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 1% chance the null hypothesis is true
A difference this large would be rare if there were truly no difference
The difference is large and important
questions.explanation: The p-value is computed assuming the null is true; it is not the probability of the null.

questions.text: Why is Welch's t-test a safer default?
options: It does not assume equal variances
It works only for large samples
questions.explanation: Welch's test remains valid when the two groups have different variances.

courses.title: Data Visualization for Official Statistics
courses.summary: Design honest, readable charts for statistical releases and dashboards.
outcomes: Match chart types to the comparison being made
Avoid common distortions such as truncated bar axes
Design accessible colour and labelling for public releases

lessons.title: Choosing the right chart
body: Start from the question, not the chart gallery:
- **Change over time** -> line chart (time on the horizontal axis).
- **Comparing categories** -> bar chart, sorted by value unless the categories have a natural order.
- **Distribution of one variable** -> histogram or box plot.
- **Relationship between two numeric variables** -> scatter plot.
Pie charts only work for a few parts of one whole; people compare lengths far more accurately than angles.

lessons.title: Honest scales
body: Bar length encodes value, so a bar chart's axis **must start at zero** - truncating it exaggerates differences. Line charts show change and may use a zoomed axis, clearly labelled.
Use the same scale when panels are meant to be compared. Show uncertainty (confidence intervals) where estimates come from samples, so readers do not over-interpret small differences.

lessons.title: Accessible design
body: About 1 in 12 men has some colour-vision deficiency. Do not rely on red vs green alone; add labels, patterns or position.
Label lines directly instead of forcing readers to a legend, keep text horizontal, and write a title that states the finding ("Rural unemployment fell in 2024") rather than the variable names.

questions.text: Best chart for monthly CPI inflation over three years?
questions.explanation: Change over time is shown most clearly with a line chart.

questions.text: To compare literacy rates across 30 districts you should use:
questions.explanation: A sorted bar chart makes category comparison easy.

questions.text: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 90%. What is the problem?
options: It exaggerates differences because bar length no longer encodes value
questions.explanation: Bars must start at zero or their lengths misrepresent the values.

questions.text: Which practice improves accessibility for colour-blind readers?
options: Adding direct labels in addition to colour
questions.explanation: Direct labels carry the meaning without relying on colour.

questions.text: Which chart title is most useful in a public release?
options: 'Urban unemployment fell for the third straight quarter'
questions.explanation: A title that states the finding tells the reader what to take away.

courses.title: Survey Design and Data Quality
courses.summary: Plan survey samples, write clear questionnaires and control data quality in the field.
outcomes: Choose between stratified, cluster and multi-stage designs
Write unambiguous questionnaire items
Detect and reduce non-response and measurement error

lessons.title: Multi-stage and cluster designs
body: Large household surveys rarely list every household in the country. Instead they use **multi-stage** designs: first select villages or urban blocks (first-stage units), then list and sample households within them.

Sampling whole clusters cuts travel cost but households in the same village tend to be similar, so each additional household adds less information. This loss is measured by the **design effect**: the ratio of the actual variance to the variance a simple random sample of the same size would give.
Stratification usually lowers variance (design effect below 1); clustering usually raises it (above 1).

lessons.title: Questionnaire design
body: Each question should measure one thing, with a clear reference period and exhaustive, mutually exclusive answer codes.
- Avoid **double-barrelled** questions ("Are you satisfied with the wage and working hours?").
- Avoid **leading** wording ("Don't you agree that...").
- Specify the **reference period** ("in the last 7 days").
Pre-test the questionnaire with a small pilot and revise items that respondents misunderstand.

lessons.title: Non-response and quality checks
body: **Unit non-response** (a household refuses) biases estimates when non-respondents differ from respondents. It is addressed through revisits, substitution rules defined in advance, and weight adjustments.
**Item non-response** (one question is skipped) is handled with imputation rules that are documented.

Build validation into data capture: range checks (age 0-120), consistency checks (a 6-year-old cannot be married), and skip-pattern checks. Monitor per-enumerator statistics to detect curbstoning (fabricated interviews).

questions.text: Why do national household surveys use multi-stage cluster designs?
options: They are always more precise than SRS
A full household list is unavailable and fieldwork cost must be controlled
They remove the need for weights
questions.explanation: Clusters make listing and travel feasible at the cost of some precision.

questions.text: A design effect of 2.0 means the design's variance is:
options: Twice that of SRS of the same size
questions.explanation: Design effect = actual variance / SRS variance.

questions.text: "Are you satisfied with your wage and working hours?" is an example of:
questions.explanation: It asks about two things, so an answer cannot be interpreted.

questions.text: Which element makes a labour-force question unambiguous?
options: A clear reference period such as 'last 7 days'
questions.explanation: Without a reference period respondents answer for different time spans.

questions.text: Which check would catch a record showing a 6-year-old as married?
questions.explanation: Consistency checks compare related fields.

questions.text: Unit non-response causes bias mainly when:
options: Non-respondents differ from respondents on what is measured
questions.explanation: Bias arises when those who do not respond are systematically different.

courses.title: Applied Statistical Data Analysis Lab
courses.summary: A hands-on lab: produce weighted estimates and a significance test from a survey extract, then interpret them.
outcomes: Compute a weighted population estimate from sampled records
Quantify uncertainty with a standard error
Test and interpret a difference between two regions

lessons.title: Planning an analysis
body: Every analysis should start with a written plan: the question, the population, the estimator, and how uncertainty will be reported. Decide these **before** looking at results to avoid choosing the method that gives the answer you hoped for.
For survey data the plan must say which weight variable is used and whether the estimate is for households or persons.

lessons.title: Estimation and uncertainty
body: Population estimate: the weighted mean sum(w*x)/sum(w). Report it with a standard error. For a simple random sample from one group, the SE of the mean is s / sqrt(n), where s is the sample standard deviation (dividing by n - 1).
When comparing two groups, compute the difference of means and its SE: sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2). Welch's t statistic is the difference divided by that SE.
A |t| value above roughly 2 (for moderate samples) indicates a difference unlikely to be due to sampling noise alone.

lessons.title: Writing up the result
body: A good write-up gives the estimate, its uncertainty, the comparison, and a plain-language conclusion with its limits: "Mean monthly consumption in Region A was Rs X (SE Y), about Z higher than Region B; the difference is statistically significant, but the sample is small and unweighted for the comparison."
Never report more decimals than the data support, and always name the data source and reference period.

questions.text: The SE of a difference between two independent means is:
questions.explanation: Variances of independent estimates add; take the square root for the SE.

questions.text: Welch's t = 3.4 for a moderate sample. The most reasonable reading is:
options: A difference unlikely to be due to sampling noise alone
questions.explanation: |t| well above 2 indicates the difference is large relative to its SE.

questions.text: For the SE of a sample mean you should compute the sample SD with divisor:
questions.explanation: The sample SD uses n - 1 (Bessel's correction). In pandas this is the default for .std().

questions.text: Why write the analysis plan before looking at results?
options: To avoid choosing methods that produce a preferred answer
questions.explanation: Pre-specifying the method protects against analyst bias.

questions.text: Which write-up is best?
options: 'Mean consumption in A was Rs 4,150 (SE 140), Rs 950 higher than B; significant, small sample.'
questions.explanation: It reports the estimate, uncertainty, comparison and limitations.

lab.title: Household consumption: Region A vs Region B
instructions: The table below is a small extract of 12 sampled households (demonstration data) with their region, sampling weight and monthly per-capita consumption in rupees.
Compute the three quantities below. You may use Python, a spreadsheet or a calculator. Numeric answers are checked automatically against the dataset with a small tolerance.
Finally, write two or three sentences interpreting the result for a non-technical reader.

tasks.label: Weighted mean monthly consumption across all 12 households (Rs)
Standard error of the (unweighted) mean for Region A, using the sample SD with n - 1 (Rs)
Welch's t statistic for (mean of A - mean of B), unweighted
